SEP (Augustine): Confessions 11 focuses on first-person experience of time, while his accounts elsewhere centre on cosmic or physical time.
problem: Aristotle did not simply leave the question open: he answered, conditionally, that if only soul can count there could be no time without soul (only change). And 'time exists only in the mind' overstates Augustine: SEP notes Confessions 11 treats time as experienced, while his other works treat cosmic time.
proposed: Aristotle asked whether there would be time if there were no soul to count it, and answered that if only a soul can count, there could be no time without soul, though change might still exist; Augustine's account in Confessions 11, which locates time in the mind's memory, attention and expectation, is often called subjectivist. (Card card.philosophy.073.c5: change 'Yet Aristotle also asked whether time would exist without a mind to count it, and left the question open. Augustine’s answer is called subjectivist: time exists only in the mind’s grasp of reality.' to 'Aristotle also asked whether time would exist without a mind to count it; if only a mind can count, he answered, there could be change but no time. Augustine’s account is often called subjectivist: he locates time in the mind’s memory, attention and expectation.')

Dialogues (Philo): 'The world plainly resembles more an animal or a vegetable, than it does a watch or a knitting-loom'; the world 'was only the first rude essay of some infant deity'.

SEP: 'Darwinian processes fueled by undesigned, unplanned, chance variations that are in turn conserved or eliminated by way of natural selection would... produce organisms exquisitely adapted to their environmental niches', unaided by intention.

Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (autobiography): 'The old argument from design in Nature, as given by Paley, which formerly seemed to me so conclusive, fails, now that the law of natural selection has been discovered.' Autobiography (Gutenberg 2010): the logic of Paley's Natural Theology 'gave me as much delight as did Euclid'.

IEP: life would not be possible if more than about two dozen properties of the universe were even slightly different; George N. Schlesinger formalizes a design inference; critics reply it is not clear no form of life would be possible, and ours may be one universe in a multiverse.

IEP: 'Darwinian theories are intended only to explain how it is that more complex living organisms developed from primordially simple living organisms, and hence do not even purport to explain the origin of the latter.'

Hume's Dialogues Part X (Philo): 'EPICURUS's old questions are yet unanswered. Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?' The claim hedges the attribution to Epicurus as traditional and uncertain.

IEP quotes Mackie (1955, p. 200): religious beliefs 'are positively irrational'; Mackie and McCloskey claim (1) God is omnipotent, (2) God is omniscient, (3) God is perfectly good and (4) evil exists cannot all be true.

SEP: in De libero arbitrio free will is 'a great good itself; but as it is not an absolute good (which is God alone) but only an intermediate one, it is liable to misuse', and hence the source of moral evil.

IEP quotes Plantinga (1974): a world of significantly free creatures who do more good than evil 'is more valuable'; God 'cannot cause or determine them to do only what is right'. SEP (Problem of Evil): a defense aims only to show no logical incompatibility, unlike a theodicy in Plantinga's sense.
IEP: 'Cancer, AIDS, famines, earthquakes... are things that happen without anybody choosing to bring them about', so the Free Will Defense cannot serve as a reason for natural evil.

IEP quotes Mackie: God could have made 'beings who would act freely but always go right'; Plantinga grants such a world is possible, but its actualization 'is not up to God alone; it also depends upon what the significantly free creatures... would do'.

SEP: 'Philosophical Investigations (PI) was published posthumously in 1953'; 'For a large class of cases... the meaning of a word is its use in the language' (PI 43), a change from meaning as representation.

PI 11 (course excerpt): tools in a toolbox: 'a hammer, pliers, a saw a screwdriver, a rule, a glue-pot, glue, nails, and screws. The functions of words are as diverse as the functions of these objects.' The fact's wording 'Think of the tools in a tool-box' follows Anscombe's 1953 printing; this excerpt is a looser transcription. SEP cites PI 11 likewise.

SEP: instead of one essential core, we should travel with the word's uses through 'a complicated network of similarities overlapping and criss-crossing' (PI 66), family resemblance, against definitive traits of form, 'be it Platonic form'.

IEP: misunderstandings are caused by analogies between forms of expression; 'I'll keep it in mind' and 'I'll keep it in this box' can make the mind seem a box whose nature 'can then seem very mysterious'; the remedy is to look at how the words are used.
SEP: 'the aim of philosophy is to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle (PI 309)'.

Commentary quotes My Philosophical Development: 'I have not found in Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations anything that seemed to me interesting and I do not understand why a whole school finds important wisdom in its pages.' IEP calls Russell his teacher.
IEP: 'Ludwig Wittgenstein is one of the most influential philosophers of the twentieth century, and regarded by some as the most important since Immanuel Kant.'

IEP: ontological arguments are non-empirical, deducing God's existence from the concept of God; SEP (Cosmological) starts from causes and contingent things in the world; SEP (Teleological) from observed design-like features.

SEP (Philippa Foot): in 'The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of Double Effect' (1967) a runaway trolley headed toward five can be diverted onto a track with one; it seems permissible to turn it. SEP (Doing vs. Allowing): the trolley driver chooses between killing one and killing five.

SEP: Foot's pair of examples: a judge must choose between framing and killing an innocent man and allowing five innocents to be killed in a riot; a trolley driver may turn onto one; the judge may not frame.

SEP: Foot argues 'the judge must choose between killing one and merely allowing five to die, while the trolley driver must choose between killing one and killing five'; SEP (Foot): negative rights carry greater weight than positive rights.

SEP: Thomson modified the case so a bystander, not the driver, chooses; the bystander chooses between killing and letting die 'and yet it still seems permissible to turn the trolley. This undermines Foot's claim'.

SEP: 'Thomson (2008) changed her mind and argued that the consensus that it is permissible for the bystander to turn the trolley was mistaken'; few would turn it onto themselves, so we may not turn it onto a stranger; 'like stealing someone's wallet to give to charity'.
SEP: pushing a bystander onto the track to stop a trolley headed for five people who cannot escape, 'examples from Thomson, 1985, based on examples in Foot 1967'.

SEP: 'Pushing another bystander onto the track to stop the trolley would be wrong, many believe. However, many believe that it would be permissible to turn a switch and divert the trolley onto a different track on which one person... is positioned.'
SEP: 'Thomas Aquinas is credited with introducing the principle of double effect' (ST II-II q.64 a.7); it distinguishes harm intended as a means from harm foreseen as a side effect.
SEP 4.5: switching makes the one's death a foreseen side effect; pushing makes a person's death part of one's plan for saving the five, a means.

SEP 4.2: the problem of closeness: it is difficult to distinguish harms foreseen as side effects from harms so close to the means that they must be intended; 'no clear resolution of this problem has emerged'.

SEP 4.5: some take the paired intuitions as proof of the means/side-effect distinction (Mikhail 2011); some argue switching is wrong (Thomson 2008); others reject that double effect explains the permissibility of switching (McIntyre 2001).
Utilitarianism.net quotes Singer (1972): 'If I am walking past a shallow pond and see a child drowning in it, I ought to wade in and pull the child out. This will mean getting my clothes muddy'.
Singer quoted: getting my clothes muddy 'is insignificant, while the death of the child would presumably be a very bad thing'; the guide: failing to save the child 'would be morally monstrous'.

Study guide premises: suffering and death from lack of food, shelter or medical care are very bad; we can prevent some by donating; the rescue principle: 'If it is in our power to prevent something very bad from happening, without thereby sacrificing anything morally significant, we ought, morally, to do it.'

Singer quoted: 'We are all in that situation of the person passing the shallow pond... the cost of a new... shirt or a night out at a restaurant or concert, can mean the difference between life and death to more than one person somewhere in the world.'

Study guide: 'What matters morally is your ability to prevent the child from dying at a low cost to yourself... regardless of how far away the child is'; geographical proximity is not inherently morally relevant.

Wikipedia: 'A common criticism of Singer's essay is the demandingness objection' (Arthur 1982, Kekes 2002, Appiah 2006). Utilitarianism.net (Demandingness): by commonsense lights charity 'is good and praiseworthy, but not obligatory'. No source opened calls it the most common criticism.
problem: The superlative 'most common criticism' is not supported; sources call it 'a common criticism'.
proposed: A common criticism of Singer's argument is the demandingness objection: commonsense morality treats charity as good but optional, and the world's needs never stop, so helping would take over your life. (Card card.philosophy.083.c5: change 'The most common criticism is the demandingness objection.' to 'A common criticism is the demandingness objection.')

evidence: Study guide (moderate rescue principle): interpreted this way, 'Singer's rescue principle would seem to allow broad leeway for reserving substantial time and resources to pursue the personal projects that are most important to us'.
SEP quotes Bentham (1780/1789, ch. xvii): 'the question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?', the line between beings whose interests count and those that do not.

IEP quotes Singer (1993: 21): 'The essence of the Principle of Equal Consideration of Interests is that we give equal weight in our moral deliberations to the like interests of all those affected by our actions', extended to animals.
SEP: 'In the 1970s, Richard Ryder coined this term... to denote a ubiquitous type of human centered prejudice, which he thought was similar to racism'; 'Peter Singer popularized the term'.

IEP: for Aristotle 'there is a natural hierarchy of living beings'; humans can use reason to guide conduct while animals rely on instinct; 'the function of animals is to serve the needs of human beings'.
SEP quotes Kant's Lectures on Ethics: we have indirect duties regarding animals, owed to humanity; 'he who is cruel to animals becomes hard also in his dealings with men'.

SEP: 'This indirect view is unsatisfying: it fails to capture the independent wrong that is being done'; IEP: Kant and Carruthers hold torturing a cat wrong because of its effect on me, which many find 'a very unsatisfying account'.
IEP: 'even granting that animals have no direct moral status, we may have (possibly demanding) duties regarding their treatment'; indirect theorists hold we ought not be cruel to animals.

Abbott's translation quotes Constant (France, 1797): the duty to speak the truth 'if it were taken singly and unconditionally, would make all society impossible'; 'To tell the truth then is a duty, but only towards him who has a right to the truth. But no man has a right to a truth that injures others.'

Constant quoted: 'a German philosopher, who goes so far as to affirm that to tell a falsehood to a murderer who asked us whether our friend, of whom he was in pursuit, had not taken refuge in our house, would be a crime'.

Kant (essay published in a Berlin periodical in 1797): 'Truth in utterances that cannot be avoided is the formal duty of a man to everyone, however great the disadvantage'; 'To be truthful (honest) in all declarations is therefore a sacred unconditional command of reason'.

Kant (Abbott): a lie 'injures another; if not another individual, yet mankind generally'; 'I cause that declarations in general find no credit'; truthfulness is 'the basis of all duties founded on contract, the laws of which would be rendered uncertain and useless if even the least exception to them were admitted'.

Kant (Abbott): if you lied that he was not in the house and he had really gone out unknown to you and met the murderer, 'you might with justice be accused as the cause of his death'; 'Whoever then tells a lie... must answer for the consequences'.

SEP (Lying): lying to a would-be murderer is permissible 'as consequentialists and moderate deontologists maintain (Constant 1964; Mill 1863; Sidgwick 1981...)'. SEP (Consequentialism): rightness 'depends only on the consequences'.

IEP: the two main papers by Nagel and Williams, 'both entitled Moral Luck, were originally published in The Aristotelian Society Supplementary... 1976'. SEP: 'their now classic pair of articles'; Williams: 'I expected to suggest an oxymoron'.
SEP quotes Kant's Groundwork (the passage Nagel cites): if the good will achieved nothing, 'like a jewel, it would still shine by itself, as something that has its full worth in itself'.

SEP: (CP) 'We are morally assessable only to the extent that what we are assessed for depends on factors under our control'; its corollary: two people differing only in factors beyond their control cannot be assessed differently.
SEP: 'if we find out that a woman who has just stepped on your toes was simply pushed, then our temptation to blame her is likely to evaporate', supporting the Control Principle.

SEP: 'two otherwise conscientious people have forgotten to have their brakes checked recently and experience brake failure, but only one of whom finds a child in the path of his car'; differential assessment is resultant moral luck.
SEP: 'Nagel identifies four kinds of luck in all: resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, and causal. Resultant luck is luck in the way things turn out.'

SEP quotes Adam Smith: 'To the intention or affection of the heart... all praise or blame... must ultimately belong'; the epistemic argument holds outcomes only give evidence of a person's intentions and commitment.
SEP: for Nagel luck affects 'not only our actions but also every intention we form and every exertion of our wills', through circumstantial and constitutive luck.

IEP: the most famous Mohist thesis is 'impartial concern' (jian'ai) 'that does not make distinctions between self and other, associates and strangers'. SEP: the guideline 'for which the Mohists are most well known is jian ai... better rendered as inclusive care'.

SEP quotes Mozi Book 16: 'Suppose people were for others' states as for their state. Then who alone would deploy his state to attack others' states?'; social harm arises from excluding others' families, cities and states from concern.

IEP: the Mohists describe a scenario in which one is about to go on a long journey and must put one's family in the care of another; they claim the obvious choice even for partialists is an impartialist.

IEP: all the case shows is 'that partialists have good reason to prefer that other people conduct themselves according to... impartial concern, rather than that they have reason to so conduct themselves, as Chad Hansen and Bryan W. Van Norden have pointed out'.

SEP (Mencius) quotes Analects 1.2: 'filial piety and respect for elders constitute the root of Goodness'; Mencius's doctrine that benevolence is achieved through 'extension' of the love first manifested in the family. SEP (Chinese Ethics): 'the doctrine of care with distinctions'.

SEP: 'Does Yi Zhi truly hold that one's affection for one's own nephew is like one's affection for a neighbor's baby?' (3A5); since humans naturally care more for relatives, a system demanding impartiality 'will be impractical'.

SEP: Mencius 'is reported to have equated inclusive care with renouncing one's father (for this reason, he dismissed Mozi as a beast)'; many later Confucian critics maintain 'that it runs counter to human nature'.

IEP: the Mohists respond that impartial concern is 'no harder than the sorts of things that rulers in the past had been able to demand and get from their subjects, such as reducing one's diet, wearing coarse clothing'.

SEP: 'the phenomenon Gregory Kavka called the precariousness of existence'; had our parents delayed their conception of a child for a few months or years, 'the odds overwhelmingly seem to favor our never having existed at all'.
SEP bases its statement of the problem and the depletion case on Parfit, Reasons and Persons (orig. 1984; cited as 1987, 361-64).

SEP 2.1: in Parfit's depletion case the community depletes rather than conserves resources; for two centuries life is 'slightly' better, after that 'the quality of life would be much lower'; conservation would have changed who is conceived.

SEP: Parfit described the person-affecting intuition as 'what is bad must be bad for someone'; with depletion it implies no one is harmed, yet 'the great lowering of the quality of life must provide some moral reason not to choose Depletion' (Parfit).
SEP 3.1 'biting the bullet' (David Boonin, 2008, 2014) and 3.2 purely impersonal views, whose paradigm example is 'classic maximizing total utilitarianism'.
SEP: 'It today remains among the most challenging problems in all of population ethics.'

SEP (Ethics of AI): 'an entity is a moral agent if and only if it has obligations, and it is a moral patient, if and only if moral agents... have obligations towards it. Humans are the typical examples of moral agents, and sentient animals the typical example of patients.'

SEP (substantive revision 2025-26): 'The standard view is that AI and robotics systems have no moral status of any kind... but this view has come under pressure'; the debate on moral status remains open.

SEP: 'there is a trend in favour of the view that sentience is at least a necessary condition for moral status (Konigs 2025)'; hence concern whether it would be ethical to create AI systems with consciousness.
SEP: creating conscious AI 'might enable sentience, and thus suffering. Some authors have called for a moratorium on synthetic phenomenology (Bentley et al. 2018; Metzinger 2021)'.

SEP: 'a relational turn has been proposed: If we relate to robots as though they had rights, then it might be futile to search whether they really do have such rights (Coeckelbergh 2010, 2012, 2018)'; Wikipedia (Robot rights): Gunkel and Coeckelbergh focus on relational ethics.
SEP: 'Bryson has insisted that robots should not enjoy rights (Bryson 2010)'.

IEP: for Kant 'autonomy is a necessary property to be the kind of being whose interests are to count directly in the moral assessment of actions'; only humans can stand back from their desires and choose.

SEP: Transplant: five patients each need a different organ; the person in Room 6, in for routine tests, is compatible with all five; the operation would save them while killing the 'donor' (Foot 1966, Thomson 1976).
SEP: classical utilitarianism implies it would not be wrong to perform the transplant; 'Most people find this result abominable', a case of overlooking the unwilling donor's right to life.

SEP: utilitarians 'can bite the bullet'; the example is so unrealistic that we should not trust our intuitions; 'Most utilitarians lack such strong stomachs... so they modify utilitarianism'; one attempt claims 'a killing is worse than a death'.
Of the Standard of Taste: 'beauty and deformity, no more than sweet and bitter, are not qualities in objects, but belong entirely to the sentiment, internal or external'. SEP dates the essay 1757.

Hume: 'Whoever would assert an equality of genius and elegance betwixt Ogilby and Milton... would be thought to defend no less an extravagance, than if he had maintained a molehill to be as high as Teneriffe'; we pronounce such sentiment 'absurd and ridiculous'.

Hume: Sancho's kinsmen judge a hogshead of wine, one detecting leather, the other iron, and are ridiculed; 'On emptying the hogshead, there was found at the bottom, an old key with a leathern thong tied to it.'

Hume: 'Strong sense, united to delicate sentiment, improved by practice, perfected by comparison, and cleared of all prejudice, can alone entitle critics to this valuable character; and the joint verdict of such... is the true standard of taste'.

SEP: Hume's proposal 'has been criticized on the grounds that it posits a viciously circular analysis of aesthetic value: aesthetically superior artworks are those endorsed by true critics, but true critics are identified by their endorsement of the best art'.

Critique of Judgement (Bernard; originally published Berlin 1790), sec. 7: if he says 'Canary wine is pleasant,' another may remind him that he ought to say 'It is pleasant to me'; as regards the pleasant, everyone has his own taste.

Critique of Judgement (Bernard), sec. 7: if he gives out anything as beautiful, 'he judges not merely for himself, but for every one'; the universal voice and the lack of any proof that can compel agreement are discussed in secs. 8 and 33.

Critique of Judgement (Bernard), sec. 2: 'The satisfaction which determines the judgement of taste is disinterested'; interest always has reference to the faculty of desire; taste in the beautiful is 'alone a disinterested and free satisfaction'.

SEP: in the Genealogy of Morals Nietzsche targets Kant's separation of pleasure in beauty from desire and 'protests that the idea of pleasure in beauty... cut-off from the particularities and idiosyncrasies of our passionate lives is unrealistic and undesirable'.

Tout-fait quotes Duchamp (1961): 'the choice of these readymades was never dictated by aesthetic delectation... The choice was based on a reaction of visual indifference with at the same time a total absence of good or bad taste'; EBSCO: Fountain (1917), a porcelain urinal, evidences that claim.

SEP: Plato holds the arts are mimetic; artworks imitate ordinary physical objects, which imitate the Forms. Republic X (Jowett): painting is 'an imitation of things... as they appear... Of appearance'; the painter is 'third in the descent from nature'.
FIU course notes on the mimetic theory: 'Music was always difficult for this theory to account for. Music doesn't seem to be imitating anything, at least on the face of it.'

IEP quotes Tolstoy: 'Art is a human activity consisting in this, that one man consciously, by means of certain external signs, hands on to others feelings he has lived through, and that others are infected by these feelings and also experience them.'
IEP (Art and Emotion): 'it is just not true that whenever a musical work is cheerful, its composer was cheerful when composing it; a sad composer could have created the work just as well.'

SEP: in an early version of Dickie's institutionalism, 'a work of art is an artifact upon which some person(s) acting on behalf of the artworld has conferred the status of candidate for appreciation (Dickie 1974)'.
SEP: 'It has also been urged that the definition's obvious circularity is vicious', given the inter-definition of artwork, artworld system, artist and artworld public.
Diogenes Laertius X (Hicks), Letter to Menoeceus: 'Accustom thyself to believe that death is nothing to us, for good and evil imply sentience, and death is the privation of all sentience'.
Hicks: 'Death, therefore, the most awful of evils, is nothing to us, seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not.'

Lucretius III (Leonard): 'Look back: Nothing to us was all fore-passed eld Of time the eternal, ere we had a birth. And Nature holds this like a mirror up Of time-to-be when we are dead and gone. And what is there so horrible appears?' SEP calls it the symmetry argument.

SEP: Thomas Nagel (1970), in his seminal essay 'Death', noted things can be bad for us by precluding goods; being made unconscious is bad for a person 'when it precedes... some joyous occasion he will miss'; death deprives us of goods.
SEP: Epictetus 'spent a portion of his life as the slave of Epaphroditus' in Rome; 'Eventually receiving his freedom, he began lecturing... He then established his own school' at Nicopolis in Greece.

Enchiridion I (Higginson): 'Within our power are opinion, aim, desire, aversion... Beyond our power are body, property, reputation, office'; take the latter for your own and 'you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed'.
Enchiridion V (Higginson): 'Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.'
SEP: Marcus 'succeeded... as Emperor of Rome in 161 CE and reigned until his death in 180'; his Meditations were 'written to and for himself'.
Meditations IV.7 (Casaubon, Gutenberg 2680): 'Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.'

SEP: 'Epictetus offers the analogy of ball players who recognize that the ball they are running after is of no value in itself, and yet exert their full energy to catch it' (2.5); externals must be used with care but with composure (2.5.6).
SEP: Marcus's Stoic life holds 'only virtue is good, only vice is bad', externals indifferent to happiness; desire is to be restricted to what is up to us (ix.7).

Nicomachean Ethics I (Gutenberg 8438): 'to constitute Happiness, there must be... complete virtue and a complete life'; the prosperous may meet great misfortunes in old age, as the tale is told of Priam, and one who died in wretchedness 'no man calls happy'.

IEP (Hedonism): prudential hedonism holds that pleasure and pain are the only things of ultimate importance for well-being; 'conscious pleasure is the only thing that positively contributes to well-being'.

SEP (Well-Being): a machine that 'would give you experiences of whatever kind you thought most valuable or enjoyable, writing a great novel...' and 'You would not know you were on the machine'; IEP cites Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), pp. 42-45.

SEP (Hedonism) quotes Nozick (1974: 43-44): it is good 'to do certain things, and not just have the experience of doing them', 'to be a certain sort of person' and not an 'indeterminate blob' floating in a tank, and 'to make a difference in the world'; 'something matters to us in addition to experience'.
IEP: in the reversed experience machine (De Brigard 2010), 'most people would choose to stay in the experience machine'; the bias thought responsible is 'the status quo bias'.

SEP: the pronouncement 'God is dead' (GS 108, 125, 343): because 'the belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable', everything 'built upon this faith', including 'the whole of our European morality', is destined for 'collapse'. The Gay Science was written in 1882 (Gutenberg editorial note).

SEP: 'The idea is not so much that atheism is true: in GS 125, he depicts this pronouncement arriving as fresh news to a group of atheists'. Gay Science 125: 'many people standing about who did not believe in God'.

Gay Science 341 'The Heaviest Burden' (Common): a demon says you must live this life 'innumerable times; and there will be nothing new in it... this spider and this moonlight among the trees'; the question 'would lie as the heaviest burden upon thy activity'.
Gay Science 341: 'Wouldst thou not throw thyself down and gnash thy teeth, and curse the demon that so spake? Or... wouldst answer him: Thou art a God, and never did I hear aught more divine!'

SEP: an influential line of readings treats it as a practical thought experiment testing whether one's life has been good, like (Maudemarie Clark's analogy) a spouse's question about whether one would marry again.
SEP: the devout Christian might affirm earthly life as a test to be redeemed by an eternal heavenly reward; 'Imagining that my finite life recurs eternally blocks this avenue'.
SEP quotes GS 276: 'I want to learn more and more to see as beautiful what is necessary in things... Amor fati: let that be my love henceforth!... someday I wish to be only a Yes-sayer.'

SEP: 'In the early reception, most readers took Nietzsche to be offering a cosmological hypothesis about the structure of time', and 'various problems have been posed for the thesis, so understood (... but cf. Loeb 2022b)'.
SEP quotes The Myth of Sisyphus: 'Deciding whether or not life is worth living is to answer the fundamental question in philosophy' (MS, 3).

SEP: Camus postulates a divorce between human consciousness, with its 'wild longing for clarity' (MS, 21), and the 'unreasonable silence of the world' (MS, 28); the absurd is this relationship, not either side alone.

SEP: rejecting suicide and hope in another life, Camus's alternative is 'to live without escape and with integrity, in revolt and defiance'; 'a life without consolation, but instead one characterized by lucidity' and awareness of its limits.
IEP: 'Doomed to eternal labor at his rock, fully conscious of the essential hopelessness of his plight, Sisyphus nevertheless pushes on'; he is 'the archetypal absurd hero'.
SEP quotes MS 123: 'The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.'

PDC: Thomas Nagel, 'The Absurd', Journal of Philosophy 68(20), October 1971, 716-727. Course handout: collision between seriousness and 'the perpetual possibility of regarding everything about which we are serious as arbitrary'; Camus's defiance may make life nobler but not less absurd; the way out is irony.

SEP (Meaning of Life): 'Supernaturalist theories are views according to which a spiritual realm is central to meaning in life'; an influential argument is that only God's purpose could be the source of invariant moral rules or objective values (Craig 1994/2013).

SEP: the objection that if God had created us with a purpose, God would have degraded us; 'in the analytic literature Kurt Baier was the first to articulate it (1957)'; rationales include that 'we would be expected to defer to the aims of a superior being'.

SEP: subjectivists hold meaning varies with a person's attitudes; one influential subjectivist holds 'life is meaningful just to the extent that one cares about or loves something (Frankfurt 1988, 2004)'.
SEP: counterexamples to subjectivism include one who 'cultivates one's prowess at long-distance spitting (Wolf 2010, 104), collects a big ball of string (Wolf 2010, 104)'.

SEP: Susan Wolf's hybrid view: 'Meaning arises when subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness' (Wolf 2015, 112); no meaning accrues from caring about a worthless project, nor from a worthwhile one one does not care about.
SEP: 'the real nub of the debate is how to answer the question Where does objective value come from?, supposing it exists'.

SEP (Death): the question is posed for lives extended indefinitely while avoiding senescence and remaining 'healthy and mentally competent'; Journal of Ethics (2015) notes Cave's distinction of medical immortals who do not age from true immortals.

SEP quotes Williams (1973, p. 83): '(1) it should clearly be me who lives forever, and (2) the state in which I survive should be one that... will be adequately related... to those aims I now have in wanting to survive at all'.

Colorado PHIL 150 notes: in the play Elina Makropulos has taken an elixir of life for 300 years; 'She is 342 years old. By this age, life has become a state of boredom, and indifference.' SEP (Death) cites 'The Makropulos Case' in Williams 1973.
SEP: for Williams, 'if we live long enough, eventually we will lose our categorical desires. At that point we will no longer be motivated to live on, and oppressive boredom will set in.'

SEP: 'Nagel (1986), Glover (1977), and Fischer (1994) have argued that the lives of superseniors need not become dull'; Williams holds varying categorical desires fails his condition that it clearly be me who lives forever.
SEP: Williams's 'claim that immortality cannot be made desirable remains controversial'.
